ideal_functionality.description: what would make this great? Describe the feature, data, or improvement that would have solved the problem.

tools.name: follow_up_create
tools.description:
Create a follow-up on an incident, either from scratch or by importing an existing external ticket.

Follow-ups are post-incident tasks — work that needs to happen after an incident is resolved, like "add monitoring for X", "update runbook", or "fix the root cause". They are distinct from in-flight actions which are checklist items used during active response. Follow-ups persist, can be assigned, prioritised, labelled, and exported to external issue trackers.

There are two modes:

1. **Create from scratch**: provide incident_id and title (required), plus optional description, assignee_id, assignee_team, priority_id, labels. The follow-up is created with status "outstanding".

2. **Import from external ticket**: provide incident_id and url (a link to an existing Linear, Jira, GitHub, GitLab, Asana, ClickUp, or Shortcut issue). The title, description, status, and assignee are imported from the ticket automatically. The follow-up is linked to the external issue for ongoing sync.

Instead of creating directly, action "suggest" posts a draft for a human to accept, edit, or decline, and action "edit_suggestion" (with suggestion_id) revises a draft. To apply a draft that was already reviewed, use action "execute" with only suggestion_id — it is applied verbatim. Prefer "suggest" when the user asked for a draft or you are unsure. In a chat conversation the draft appears as a card; elsewhere it has no card — show it to the user, and find it later with suggestion_list. A url import cannot be drafted.

If the org requires a priority or assignee, those fields become required and the tool will return a validation error if they're missing. A draft is looser: a missing required assignee is filled for you (the incident lead, else the caller), and a required priority is enforced when a person accepts.

A user and a team can own a follow-up at the same time. Omit assignee_team and the incident's own team is used where the organisation requires one; pass an empty string for no team. Where the organisation demands a team and none can be inferred, the call is refused rather than creating one it considers invalid.

assignee_id, assignee_team and priority_id each take an ID or a name. A name matching more than one user, team or priority is rejected rather than guessed.

incident_id.description: incident to create the follow-up on (ID, external ID, or reference like INC-123)

action.description: 'execute' (default) creates the follow-up directly, or applies a reviewed draft when only suggestion_id is passed; 'suggest' posts a draft for a human to accept, edit, or decline; 'edit_suggestion' revises an existing draft

suggestion_id.description: the draft to act on — required with 'edit_suggestion', and with 'execute' to apply a draft that was already reviewed. Accepts an id from a suggest result or suggestion_list. On an edit, omitted fields keep the draft's current values

title.description: follow-up title describing the action needed (required unless url is provided)

assignee_id.description: user ID or name to assign the follow-up to (find ids with user_list). A name matching more than one user is rejected rather than guessed

assignee_team.description: team catalog entry ID or name to own this follow-up (find teams with catalog_entry_list). A user and a team can own one at the same time. Omit to take the incident's own team where the organisation sets one; pass an empty string for no team

priority_id.description: follow-up priority ID or name (see config://organisation for IDs)

labels.description: labels to attach (max 50 chars each, created automatically if new)

url.description: URL of an existing issue in an external tracker (Linear, Jira, GitHub, etc.) to import as a follow-up — when provided, title and description are fetched from the ticket automatically (action 'execute' only)

tools.name: follow_up_list
tools.description:
List follow-ups with optional filters and pagination.

Follow-ups are post-incident tasks that track work needed after an incident is resolved — things like "add monitoring for X", "update runbook", or "fix the root cause". They are distinct from in-flight actions (checklist items used during active response). Follow-ups can have priorities, assignees, labels, and can be exported to external issue trackers like Jira or Linear.

Each result includes: title, status, priority, assignee (user), assignee team, creator, labels, linked external issue, and timestamps.

Filters (all optional):
- incident_id: filter to a specific incident (accepts ID, external ID, or reference like INC-123)
- assignee_id: filter by assignee user ID (use your own ID from config://organisation to find "my follow-ups")
- assignee_team_id: filter to a team (a catalog entry ID from team_list). Matches follow-ups assigned to the team, plus follow-ups assigned to a direct member of that team when no team is set — mirroring what the team page shows. An explicit team assignment always wins.
- status: one or more of outstanding, completed, not_doing
- created_after / created_before: date range for when the follow-up was created (yyyy-mm-dd or RFC 3339). Useful for scoping to recent follow-ups rather than returning historical items.

Pagination: results are ordered oldest first. Use page_size (default 10, max 50) and pass "next_cursor" as "after" to fetch subsequent pages. Stopping before "has_more" is false means you have incomplete results.

For aggregate counts and breakdowns (e.g. "how many outstanding follow-ups by priority?"), use follow_up_stats instead of paginating through this list.

For post-incident review workflows, combine with incident_show to understand the incident context behind each follow-up. Use follow_up_create to add new follow-ups discovered during analysis.

after.description: cursor from a previous page to fetch the next one

incident_id.description: filter to a specific incident (ID, external ID, or reference like INC-123)

assignee_team_id.description: filter by owning team — a catalog entry ID from the org's Team catalog type (use team_list to discover valid IDs)

status.description: filter by status: outstanding, completed, not_doing

created_after.description: only follow-ups created after this date (yyyy-mm-dd or RFC 3339)

created_before.description: only follow-ups created before this date (yyyy-mm-dd or RFC 3339)

tools.name: follow_up_stats
tools.description:
Count follow-ups grouped by one or more dimensions, returning aggregate statistics.

Use this tool when you need counts or breakdowns across many follow-ups — for example "how many outstanding follow-ups by priority?" or "follow-up completion rate by incident severity". Use follow_up_list to browse individual follow-ups.

Dimensions (combine freely in the group_by array):
- status: group by follow-up status (outstanding, completed, not_doing)
- priority: group by follow-up priority (e.g. P0, P1, P2). Shows "No priority" for unset.
- assignee: group by assigned user. Shows "Unassigned" for follow-ups without an assignee.
- has_external_issue: group by whether the follow-up has been exported to an external tracker like Jira or Linear (true/false)
- incident_severity: group by the severity of the parent incident (e.g. Critical, Major, Minor). Useful for answering "are we completing follow-ups from our most critical incidents?"
- week: group by ISO week (e.g. 2026-W03)
- month: group by calendar month (e.g. 2026-01)
- quarter: group by calendar quarter (e.g. 2026-Q1)

Each group includes a count, sample incident references (e.g. INC-123) for drill-down, an age summary for outstanding items showing how long they've been open, and a completion-time summary (mean and max days from creation to completion) covering the group's completed follow-ups. Completion time is measured for follow-ups created within the queried window; narrowing by created_after/created_before therefore answers "how long did the follow-ups created in this period take to close".

By default, deleted and archived follow-ups are excluded.

The tool processes at most 25,000 follow-ups. If more match, the response sets "truncated": true — narrow the date range for accurate results.

Drill-down: each group includes incident references. Pass these to follow_up_list(incident_id: "INC-123") to see the individual follow-ups, or to incident_show for incident context.

Cross-reference: use incident_stats to understand the incidents that generated these follow-ups, and follow_up_list to browse and update individual items.

Structured analysis: for a comprehensive report with playbooks and recommendations, call analysis_start first.

group_by.description: dimensions to group by. Categorical: status (outstanding/completed/not_doing), priority, assignee, has_external_issue (exported to Jira/Linear/etc). Parent incident: incident_severity. Time buckets: week, month, quarter. If empty, returns a single total count.

status.description: filter by follow-up status: outstanding, completed, not_doing

incident_id.description: filter to a specific incident (ID, external ID, or reference like INC-123)

priority.description: filter by follow-up priority option IDs

created_after.description: only follow-ups created after this date (yyyy-mm-dd or RFC 3339)

created_before.description: only follow-ups created before this date (yyyy-mm-dd or RFC 3339)

max_sample_ids_per_group.description: how many incident references (e.g. INC-123) to return per group (default 10, max 250). Set to 0 to omit IDs entirely.

sort_groups_by.description: order groups by: alphabetical (the default — by dimension key, so week/month/quarter come back chronological) or count (highest first). max_groups keeps the first N groups in the current order, so to get a true top-N (e.g. assignees with the most outstanding follow-ups) pass count — otherwise you get an alphabetical slice that can omit the largest groups.

max_groups.description: limit the number of groups returned (e.g. top 10). Check total_groups in the response to see how many existed before truncation.

tools.name: follow_up_update
tools.description:
Update an existing follow-up. Only the fields you provide will be changed — omitted fields are left as-is.

Use follow_up_list to find follow-up IDs. Use follow_up_create to add new follow-ups.

Updatable fields:
- title: rename the follow-up
- description: set or clear the description (empty string clears)
- assignee_id: assign to a user by ID or name (empty string unassigns the user)
- assignee_team: set the owning team by catalog entry ID or name (empty string unassigns the team)
- priority_id: set priority by ID or name (empty string clears, see config://organisation for IDs)
- status: change to outstanding, completed, or not_doing
- labels: replace all labels (omit to leave unchanged)

A user and a team can own a follow-up at the same time: assignee_id and assignee_team are independent, and setting one never clears the other. A name matching more than one user, team or priority is rejected rather than guessed.

Deleting a follow-up is not possible here, so "deleted" is not an accepted status.

If the follow-up has been exported to an external issue tracker (Jira, Linear, etc.), the fields that sync from the external system cannot be changed here and the tool says which they are. The owning team can always be changed; the priority can too, unless the organisation syncs priorities from the tracker.

Returns the updated follow-up.

description.description: new description (pass empty string to clear)

assignee_id.description: user ID or name to assign (pass empty string to unassign the user; the owning team is left alone)

assignee_team.description: team catalog entry ID or name to own this follow-up (pass empty string to unassign the team; the assigned user is left alone)

priority_id.description: follow-up priority ID or name (pass empty string to clear, see config://organisation for IDs)

status.description: new status: outstanding, completed, or not_doing

labels.description: replace all labels (max 50 chars each, omit to leave unchanged)

tools.name: help_query
tools.description:
Ask how incident.io works and get an answer written from incident.io's own product documentation.

Use it for questions about the product itself: "how do escalation paths work?", "what does incident.io integrate with for follow-ups?", "how do I set up an alert route?", "what's the difference between streams and incidents?". Reach for it before guessing at product behaviour, and before telling a user something isn't possible.

This is not document_search. document_search searches the organisation's own synced documents — their runbooks, guides and post-mortems from GitHub, Notion or Confluence. This tool searches incident.io's documentation of the product, which every organisation shares and none can add to. A question about how a feature behaves belongs here; a question about how this organisation responds to an outage belongs in document_search.

It answers from documentation only and can see nothing about the organisation — no incidents, schedules or configuration. For "who is on call right now?" or "which alert routes do we have?", use the tools that read live data.

Returns a written answer, not a list of matching documents: there are no per-document ids to read further, so ask a fuller question than you would give a search box. A model writes the answer, so a call takes a few seconds.

Pass session_id from a previous response to ask a follow-up with the earlier turns in context.

question.description: the question about incident.io, phrased as you would ask a support engineer (e.g. 'how do escalation paths pick who to page?')

session_id.description: resume a previous help conversation by passing the session_id from a prior response

tools.name: incident_create
tools.description:
Create a new incident.

Use this tool when you know what incident to create (e.g. from an alert, a customer report, or a detected issue).

Before creating from an alert or a report, check for an existing open (triage, active
or paused) incident for the same problem so you attach to it or merge rather than
declaring a duplicate.

Required: name (a short, descriptive title).

A retry of the same request returns the incident it already created, with already_existed set — say it was already declared rather than claiming you declared it.

Rate limited: an organisation can only create a limited number of incidents per hour.
A call over the limit is rejected — don't retry in a loop.

The incident is created in triage by default — this means no severity is required and the team can assess before accepting. To create an already-accepted incident, provide both severity_id and an active incident_status_id.

**Never invent a severity.** Only pass severity_id if the user has explicitly stated one (e.g. "create a sev2", "this is critical"). If they haven't, leave severity_id empty so the incident starts in triage and a responder can set it later.

Some organisations have disabled manual triage incidents — those require severity_id at creation time. The organisation's declare form may also require custom fields on every incident, including triage.

A call missing any required field creates nothing.

If the tool can deliver the form to the person itself, the call succeeds and says what was missing — tell them the form is waiting for them and stop; don't repeat the field list or claim you declared anything.

Otherwise it returns a "missing_required_fields" validation error. Its first entry summarises what is missing. After it comes one "missing_required_field" entry per field, each pointing at the field it means: severity_id for severity, custom_field_entries/<custom_field_id> for a custom field. Read those pointers to tell the fields apart.

You may be given a URL to a form that the user can fill in the missing fields which you should share with them to complete if you cannot gather the fields yourself. If they tell you what all of the missing fields should be you can retry calling the tool with those new fields.

Defaults applied when fields are omitted:
- visibility: public
- incident_type_id: the organisation's default incident type
- incident_status_id: triage (only if the organisation allows manual triage incidents)
- severity_id: none (allowed in triage; required if status is active or if the org has disabled manual triage)
- slack_team_id: only meaningful on Slack Enterprise Grid with multiple workspaces — defaults to the workspace the authenticated user is a member of (when unambiguous), otherwise the organisation's primary workspace

Read the config://organisation resource to discover severity IDs, status IDs, incident type IDs, custom field IDs, and role IDs.

Returns the created incident summary.

name.description: short, descriptive incident name (e.g. 'Database connection pool exhausted')

summary.description: initial summary describing what is happening (markdown)

severity_id.description: severity ID (see config://organisation), or the catalog entry ID for a severity. If omitted, the incident starts in triage with no severity — set severity when you accept it.

incident_status_id.description: status ID to start in (see config://organisation). Defaults to triage. If you set an active status, severity_id is required.

incident_type_id.description: incident type ID (see config://organisation). Defaults to the organisation's default type.

visibility.description: public (default, visible to all) or private (restricted access)

slack_team_id.description: Slack workspace (team) ID to create the incident channel in, e.g. T012AB3CD4. Only relevant for Slack Enterprise Grid organisations with multiple workspaces — see the Slack workspaces section of config://organisation. Omit otherwise.

users_to_invite.description: user IDs to invite to the incident channel . These must be incident.io user IDs — any other kind of ID invites nobody, with no error. Ignored for private incidents.

value_option_id.description: for option-type fields: the option ID

value_catalog_entry_id.description: for catalog-type fields: the catalog entry ID

value_text.description: for text-type fields: the text value

value_numeric.description: for numeric-type fields: the numeric value as a string

values.description: values to set. Use an empty array to clear the field.

custom_field_entries.description: custom field values to set on the new incident

incident_role_id.description: ID of the incident role (see config://organisation)

user_id.description: user ID to assign. Omit to unassign the current holder.

role_assignments.description: role assignments for the new incident (see config://organisation for role IDs)

tools.name: incident_list
tools.description:
Search and list incidents, returning a summary per result. Use incident_show to get full details for a specific incident.

Each result includes: reference (e.g. INC-123), name, status (with category), severity, mode, reported_at, updated_at, and a permalink. A merged incident (status category "merged") also includes "merged_into", identifying the incident it was merged into.

Use the include parameter to enrich results with additional fields, avoiding the need to call incident_show for each incident:
- summary: short incident summary (~200 chars, AI-generated or human-written) — useful for understanding what each incident was about without fetching full details
- roles: include role assignments (e.g. incident lead) with user names and IDs
- custom_fields: include custom field values
- timestamps: named timestamps (e.g. reported at, resolved at) — useful for timeline and trend analysis
- durations: duration metrics (e.g. time to resolve, in seconds) — useful for comparing incident response times
- escalation_urgency: include AI assessment of whether each incident needed immediate response (urgency level and tags). Only available for orgs with AI investigations enabled. Use incident_show for the full reasoning text.

This is especially useful for analytical queries like "who has been incident lead the most?" — include roles and paginate through the results rather than calling incident_show for each one. For trend analysis, include summary, timestamps, and durations to get context without extra API calls.

By default only standard and retrospective incidents are returned, and declined/canceled/merged incidents are excluded. Provide explicit filters to override these defaults.

Filters (all optional):
- query: free-text search across incident names
- status_category: one or more of triage, active, post-incident, closed, paused, declined, merged, canceled
- severity: one or more severity IDs
- incident_type: one or more incident type IDs (e.g. filter to "Default" only, or exclude "Internal" and "Maintenance")
- mode: one or more of standard, retrospective, test, tutorial. standard is a real, live incident; retrospective records something that already happened for the postmortem/timeline without a live response; test and tutorial are practice incidents (a test run, or the onboarding walkthrough) and are excluded by default
- team: one or more team IDs (exact match — incidents tagged with any of these teams)
- team_part_of: one or more team IDs including all sub-teams in the hierarchy (e.g. "Platform" returns incidents for Platform and all its child teams). Mutually exclusive with team.
- custom_fields: filter by custom field values (object mapping field ID to array of value IDs)
- created_after / created_before: dates to bound the time range (yyyy-mm-dd or RFC 3339)
- assigned_to: one or more user IDs (or the literal "me" for the calling user). Returns incidents where any listed user is a participant (responder/collaborator/observer) or has any incident role assignment (e.g. lead). Use this to triage your own workload without wading through everyone else's, e.g. {"assigned_to": ["me"], "status_category": ["triage", "active"]}. "me" only works for OAuth tokens, not API keys.

To discover severity IDs, incident type IDs, custom field IDs, and custom field value IDs, read the config://organisation resource first.

Sorting: results are ordered newest first by default. Set sort_by to "workload" to order by total responder-minutes (highest first), which is useful for finding the most costly incidents. Workload data is synced hourly from our insights pipeline.

Pagination: use page_size to control the page (default 10, max 50). When the response has "has_more": true, pass the "next_cursor" value as "after" to fetch the next page. Stopping before "has_more" is false means you have incomplete results.

Tip: if you need counts or trend data, use incident_stats first — it's much more efficient than paginating through incident_list and counting manually. Use incident_list when you need to browse individual records or need the detail that includes provide.

after.description: cursor from a previous page to fetch the next one

sort_by.description: sort order: created_at (default, newest first) or workload (highest total responder-minutes first, uses insights data synced hourly)

status_category.description: filter by status category: triage, active, post-incident, closed, paused, declined, merged, canceled

incident_type.description: filter by incident type ID (read config://organisation to discover type IDs)

mode.description: filter by mode: standard, retrospective, test, tutorial

team.description: filter by team IDs (exact match). Mutually exclusive with team_part_of. Use team_list to discover team IDs.

team_part_of.description: filter by team IDs including all sub-teams in the hierarchy. Use this when you want incidents for a team and all its descendant teams. Mutually exclusive with team. Use team_list to discover team IDs.

custom_fields.description: filter by custom field values: keys are custom field IDs, values are arrays of accepted value IDs (read the config://organisation resource to discover field and value IDs)

created_after.description: only incidents created after this date (yyyy-mm-dd or RFC 3339)

created_before.description: only incidents created before this date (yyyy-mm-dd or RFC 3339)

The literal string "me" resolves to the calling user (only available for OAuth tokens, not API keys). Useful for triaging your own workload — e.g. {"assigned_to": ["me"], "status_category": ["triage", "active"]} returns your open incidents. Use the "You" section of config://organisation to find your own user ID, or team_list / team_show to find other users' IDs.

include.description: optional fields to enrich each result with: summary (short incident summary, ~200 chars), roles (role assignments), custom_fields (custom field values), timestamps (named timestamps like reported at, resolved at), durations (duration metrics like time to resolve), escalation_urgency (AI assessment of whether immediate response was needed — urgency and tags only, use incident_show for full reasoning). Use these to avoid calling incident_show for every result.

tools.name: incident_merge
tools.description:
Merge incidents that turn out to be the same problem into one.

The incidents in incident_ids are the sources: each moves to the merged status and stops being responded to separately. merged_into_incident_id is the target, which survives and carries the response on. Merging several sources into one target is a single call — don't loop.

A source must currently be in triage, active or paused. Anything else — already merged, resolved, closed, declined, cancelled — is refused. The target must not itself have been merged into something else: merge into the incident at the end of that chain instead. Streams cannot be merged, on either side.

Every source is checked before any of them is merged, so a refusal leaves all of them untouched — which is why the sources belong in one call rather than one call each. The merges themselves apply one at a time rather than as a single transaction, so if one does fail after the checks have passed, the merges before it stand. Call again with the same list to see where it got to: an incident that already merged is refused by name.

Merging is visible to responders: each source's channel is archived after a delay, its alerts and attachments move onto the target, and its subscribers are notified.

Read the result with incident_show. To reverse a merge, use incident_unmerge on the source that was merged away.

incident_ids.description: the incidents to merge away — the sources (ID, external ID, or reference like INC-123). Each must currently be in triage, active or paused.

merged_into_incident_id.description: the incident they are merged into — the target, which survives (ID, external ID, or reference like INC-123)

tools.name: incident_message
tools.description:
Share a finding, insight, or piece of analysis into an incident's chat channel, so the responders can see it.

Posts a quoted message attributed to you, with an optional threaded reply for longer detail. Use it to forward something you have worked out — "post that to the channel", "let the responders know".

This is not the tool for updating the incident. Three nearby things go elsewhere:
- Communicating a change to status, severity, summary or custom fields, or a progress note on the incident timeline, is incident_update (its message field).
- Correcting an in-progress investigation's hypothesis is investigation_steer.
- Answering the user in this conversation needs no tool at all.

Distil the key finding into a concise message rather than dumping the whole conversation. The main message is quoted in the channel, so keep it to the takeaway and put supporting detail in thread_message.

The attribution line names you from your credentials — it cannot be set by the caller. An incident with no chat channel has nowhere to post, and is refused.

incident_id.description: incident whose channel to post into (ID, external ID, or reference like INC-123)

message.description: the finding to post, in markdown. Keep it concise — distil the key takeaway rather than pasting the whole conversation.

thread_message.description: optional longer detail posted as a threaded reply, so the main message stays concise

tools.name: incident_show
tools.description:
Look up an incident by ID or reference (e.g. INC-123, 123, or a full ID) and return its details.

Returns: name, status, severity, roles, participants, custom fields, timestamps, durations, workload (responder time split by working/late/overnight hours), summaries, channel URLs, and the 5 most recent status updates. For a merged incident, "merged_into" identifies the incident it was merged into.

Use 'include' to request additional sections:
- investigation: AI investigation findings and extended summary. Always request this when investigating root causes or triaging — it contains the analysis our AI has already performed.
- postmortem: the post-mortem document content. Request this when reviewing what happened or preparing reports — it contains the team's written analysis.
- updates: all status updates (default returns most recent 5 only). Request this when you need the full timeline of how the incident progressed.
- escalation_urgency: AI assessment of whether the incident truly needed immediate response (immediate, deferrable, or unsure) with classification tags and reasoning. Useful for on-call burden analysis and alert noise reviews. Only available for orgs with AI investigations enabled.
- call_notes: AI-generated notes from calls, returned as two separate lists. "call_notes" covers calls held during the incident — what responders said while working it. "meeting_notes" covers follow-up meetings held afterwards, such as debriefs and post-mortem reviews. Request this when you want what people actually discussed rather than what was written down. Notes are only returned for the 5 most recent calls; raw transcripts are not available through this API.

For investigation or root cause analysis, request include: ["investigation", "postmortem"] — the default response without these only gives you the basic metadata, not the deeper analysis.

For the full investigation content (all findings, checks, conversation history, and incident context as a file tree), use the investigation_sync tool instead — it returns a downloadable tar.gz archive of the complete investigation filesystem.

id.description: incident ID, external ID, or reference (e.g. INC-123, 123, or a ULID)

include.description: optional sections to include: postmortem, investigation, updates, escalation_urgency, call_notes

tools.name: incident_stats
tools.description:
Count incidents grouped by one or more dimensions, returning aggregate statistics.

Use this tool when you need counts, breakdowns, or trend data across many incidents — for example "how many P1s this quarter?" or "incident volume by team by month". Use incident_list when you need to browse or search individual incidents, and incident_show to get full details for a specific incident.

Dimensions (combine freely in the group_by array):
- severity: group by severity level (e.g. Critical, Major, Minor)
- status: group by status category (e.g. triage, active, closed)
- type: group by incident type
- mode: group by mode. standard is a live incident, retrospective records a past one for its postmortem/timeline, and test/tutorial are practice incidents (excluded by default)
- alert_source: group by the alert source that triggered the incident (e.g. Datadog, Sentry). Shows "No alert" for manually created incidents. Multi-value: incidents with alerts from multiple sources are counted under each source individually.
- escalation_urgency: group by AI-assessed urgency (immediate, deferrable, unsure, or "Not assessed" for incidents without analysis). Useful for quantifying alert noise and on-call burden — combine with month for trend analysis.
- team: group by the org's configured team (e.g. Engineering, Platform). Prefer this over grouping by a team-shaped custom field (custom_field:<id>) — "team" resolves the org's configured team field, so its counts agree with filtering by team. Multi-value: incidents tagged with several teams are counted under each; incidents with no team show as "None". Combine with month/severity for per-team trends and workload.
- custom_field:<field_id>: group by a custom field's values (read config://organisation to find field IDs). Multi-value: multi-select fields are flattened so each value is counted individually.
- role:<role_id>: group by who is assigned a specific role (e.g. Incident Lead). Shows user names, or "Unassigned" for incidents without that role.
- week: group by ISO week (e.g. 2026-W03)
- month: group by calendar month (e.g. 2026-01)
- quarter: group by calendar quarter (e.g. 2026-Q1)

Each group includes a count, a workload breakdown (total responder-minutes split by working hours, late evening, and overnight), and the most recent incident references (e.g. INC-123) which you can pass directly to incident_show to drill into. Workload data is synced hourly from our insights pipeline and may be absent for very recent incidents.

By default, test and tutorial incidents are excluded and declined/canceled/merged incidents are excluded. Provide explicit status_category or mode filters to override these defaults.

The tool processes at most 25,000 incidents. If more match, the response sets "truncated": true — narrow the date range for accurate results.

Drill-down: each group includes incident references (e.g. INC-123). Pass these to incident_show with include: ["investigation", "postmortem"] to understand root causes behind the numbers.

Cross-reference: compare with alert_stats(group_by: ["source"]) to see how alert volume and noise translate to the incident workload shown here.

Structured analysis: for a comprehensive report with playbooks, themes, and recommendations, call analysis_start first — it provides step-by-step methodology and a branded report template. Use this tool directly only for quick, focused queries.

group_by.description: dimensions to group by, e.g. ["severity", "month"]. Categorical: severity, status, type, mode, escalation_urgency, team. Custom field: custom_field:<field_id>. Time buckets: week, month, quarter. If empty, returns a single total count.

status_category.description: filter by status category: triage, active, post-incident, closed, paused, declined, merged, canceled

incident_type.description: filter by incident type ID (read config://organisation to discover type IDs)

mode.description: filter by mode: standard, retrospective, test, tutorial

team.description: filter by team IDs (exact match). Mutually exclusive with team_part_of. Use team_list to discover team IDs.

team_part_of.description: filter by team IDs including all sub-teams in the hierarchy. Mutually exclusive with team. Use team_list to discover team IDs.

custom_fields.description: filter by custom field values: keys are custom field IDs, values are arrays of accepted value IDs

created_after.description: only incidents created after this date (yyyy-mm-dd or RFC 3339)

created_before.description: only incidents created before this date (yyyy-mm-dd or RFC 3339)

max_incident_ids_per_group.description: how many incident references (e.g. INC-123) to return per group (default 10, max 250). Set to 0 to omit IDs entirely.

sort_groups_by.description: order groups by: alphabetical (the default — by dimension key, so week/month/quarter come back chronological), count (highest first), or workload (highest total responder-minutes first). max_groups keeps the first N groups in the current order, so to get a true top-N (e.g. busiest teams) pass count or workload — otherwise you get an alphabetical slice that can omit the largest groups.

tools.name: incident_unmerge
tools.description:
Reverse a merge, restoring an incident as a standalone incident.

It operates on the incident that was merged away — the source. You don't say what it was merged into: that is derived from the incident's own history. The incident is restored to the status it held before the merge, falling back to triage if it was merged straight out of triage.

Only an incident currently in a merged status can be unmerged. Anything else — active, closed, declined, never merged at all — is refused rather than changed.

Unmerging is visible to responders: the incident's channel is un-archived if the merge was recent enough, the attachments copied onto the merge target are detached again, and subscribers are notified of the status change.

Read the incident with incident_show afterwards to see which status it was restored to. To merge incidents in the first place, use incident_merge.

incident_id.description: the incident that was merged away and should be restored (ID, external ID, or reference like INC-123). This is the source of the merge, not the incident it was merged into.

tools.name: incident_update
tools.description:
Update an incident: post a status update message, rename it, change its summary, severity or status, set custom fields, assign roles, or set incident timestamps. Only the fields you provide change — omitted fields are left as-is.

Set everything the user asked for in a SINGLE call: accepting an incident, setting its summary, posting a message and pausing it all go in one call.

Choose an action:
- action "execute" (the default) applies the change directly. Use it when the user asks you to make a change or post an update, or gives the exact content. To apply a draft that was already reviewed, pass only suggestion_id — execute it verbatim, without adding fields the user didn't approve.
- action "suggest" drafts the change for a human to accept, edit or decline. Use it when the user wants an update written or drafted rather than posted, wants your opinion on a name, or is vague ("update pls") — don't ask for clarification, just draft sensible fields. In a chat conversation the draft appears as a card; elsewhere it has no card, so show it to the user yourself and find it later with suggestion_list.
- action "edit_suggestion" revises a draft. Pass suggestion_id and the fields to change.

An "execute" that can't be applied yet changes nothing, and comes back one of two ways. Usually a draft is made for you — accepting a triage incident with no severity or incident type, or resolving and closing, which send the user through the required-fields form — and "suggestion" carries it: relay it, don't retry. Otherwise the result names required fields that are unset and asks you to draft it, and there is no "suggestion": call again once with action "suggest", filling those fields from context rather than asking the user for them.

This tool posts a real, user-visible update and is NOT idempotent, so read "incident" on the result to tell what happened. Once it is set the change is applied: never call the tool again for that request — if part of the change didn't land, tell the user. A result without it applied nothing and doesn't count against that, whether it was rejected, drafted, or asked you to draft: act on what it says and call again at most once.

Status transitions follow the incident lifecycle:
- From triage you can accept (move to an active status), pause, decline, resolve or close (the last two decline it). Declining is only possible from triage.
- From active you can pause, resolve, close, cancel, or move to another active status. You can't move an active incident back to triage.
- Pausing a triage incident works in one call — it's accepted first automatically. Don't split it into two steps.
- You can't reopen a closed, merged or cancelled incident. A declined incident must be reopened (moved back to triage or to an active status) before any other change.

Accepting an incident requires an incident type. Incidents declared from alerts often have none, so pass incident_type_id alongside incident_status in the same call — it can only be set while still in triage.

Resolving may require custom fields: some organisations require certain fields before an incident can be resolved. Set them with custom_fields in the same call — otherwise nothing is applied and the result names the fields for you to draft with.

This tool cannot merge incidents (use incident_merge), update a status page (use status_page_update), or update an action or follow-up. To have the change decided for you rather than specified, use ask_incident.

Read config://organisation to discover severity, status, incident type, custom field, role and timestamp IDs.

incident_id.description: incident to update (ID, external ID, or reference like INC-123)

action.description: 'execute' (default) applies the change directly; 'suggest' drafts it for a human to accept, edit or decline; 'edit_suggestion' revises an existing draft. An execute that can't be applied yet is drafted for you rather than refused

suggestion_id.description: the draft to act on — required with 'edit_suggestion', and with 'execute' to post a draft that was already reviewed. Accepts an id from a suggest result, suggestion_list, or ask_incident. On an edit, omitted fields keep the draft's current values

message.description: status update message to post to the incident channel (markdown). A point-in-time note to the team, distinct from the summary. Omit when no written update is needed

summary.description: new incident summary (markdown). Not supported on streams

severity.description: severity to set, by name or ID (see config://organisation). Never invent one: only set this if a severity has been explicitly stated. Not supported on streams

incident_status.description: status to move the incident to — a status name or ID (see config://organisation), or an intent word: 'accept' (the first active status), 'resolve', or 'close'. Prefer the intent words: 'resolve' routes to the right destination (a triage incident is declined, a required post-incident flow is entered, otherwise the incident is closed) and 'close' skips a required post-incident flow, which only users with permission to opt out can do; for anyone else it enters the flow like 'resolve'. Don't name a post-incident or closed status for a resolve/close request

unpause_at.description: RFC 3339 timestamp for when a paused incident should automatically unpause (e.g. 2026-03-20T14:30:00Z). Required when moving to a paused status, unless the incident is already paused

incident_type_id.description: incident type ID to set (see config://organisation). Can only be set while the incident is in triage. Accepting an incident requires one, so set it alongside incident_status when the incident has none

role.description: the incident role to assign, by name or ID (see config://organisation)

user_id.description: user ID to assign to the role (find ids with user_list). Omit to unassign whoever currently holds it

timestamp.description: the incident timestamp to set, by name or ID (see config://organisation)

value.description: RFC 3339 timestamp to set it to (e.g. 2026-03-20T14:30:00Z). Omit to clear it

timestamps.description: incident timestamps to set or clear

custom_field_id.description: ID of the custom field (see config://organisation)

option_value.description: for option fields: the option's value or ID

catalog_entry_id.description: for catalog fields: the entry's ID, external ID, or alias — never its display name. Resolve a name with catalog_entry_list first

text_value.description: for text fields: the text value

numeric_value.description: for numeric fields: the numeric value as a string

values.description: values to set. Use an empty array to clear the field

update_mode.description: how to combine with the field's existing values: 'set' replaces all (default), 'merge' adds to them (multi-value fields only)

custom_fields.description: custom field values to set. Not supported on streams

tools.name: incident_update_list
tools.description:
List status updates for an incident, most recent first.

Each update shows the message, any status or severity change, and when it was posted. The update that merged the incident also includes "merged_into", the incident it was merged into. The incident_show tool returns the 5 most recent updates by default — use this tool when you need the full history.

Pagination: use page_size (default 10, max 50) and pass "next_cursor" as "after" to fetch subsequent pages. Stopping before "has_more" is false means you have incomplete results.

incident_id.description: incident ID, external ID, or reference (e.g. INC-123, 123, or a ULID)

after.description: cursor from a previous page to fetch the next one

tools.name: investigation_feedback
tools.description:
Record a user's overall feedback on an AI investigation — whether it was helpful in responding to the incident. Feedback can only be submitted once the incident is resolved.

Provide either incident_id (ID, external ID, or reference like INC-123) or investigation_id. When using incident_id, the most recent completed investigation for that incident is selected.

Set sentiment to "helpful", "not_helpful", or "not_seen" (the user didn't use the investigation). Optionally include reasons matching the sentiment, plus a freeform comment (a comment can accompany any sentiment). Valid reasons per sentiment:
- helpful: root_cause_correct, pointed_right_direction, gathered_context, caught_something_missed, confirmed_thinking
- not_helpful: not_accurate, too_late, too_frequent, missing_information, didnt_do_what_asked, already_knew
- not_seen: already_knew, too_late, too_frequent, work_elsewhere

IMPORTANT: This submits feedback on the user's behalf. Always confirm the sentiment (and any reasons/comment) with the user before calling this tool — don't infer their verdict and submit it unprompted.

incident_id.description: incident ID, external ID, or reference (e.g. INC-123). Resolves to the latest investigation for this incident.

investigation_id.description: specific investigation ID to give feedback on. Use this if you already know the investigation ID.

sentiment.description: overall verdict on the investigation: 'helpful', 'not_helpful', or 'not_seen' (the user didn't use it)

reasons.description: optional reasons matching the sentiment — see the tool description for the valid options per sentiment

comment.description: optional freeform comment expanding on the feedback

tools.name: investigation_start
tools.description:
Start an AI SRE investigation for an incident.

An investigation runs automated checks in the background to gather context about the incident — telemetry, recent code changes, similar past incidents — and builds a hypothesis from what it finds. Use this when you want investigation artifacts or telemetry for an incident and nothing is investigating it yet.

Pass incident_id as an ID, external ID, or reference like INC-123, exactly as investigation_steer accepts it.

Starting an investigation is visible to responders, and neither effect comes back in this result: a summary message is posted and pinned into the incident's chat channel, and the user whose credentials made the call is invited into that channel. Credentials with no user attached — an API key — start an investigation attributed to nobody, and invite nobody.

If an investigation is already running for the incident this returns started: false with that investigation's ID rather than starting a second one. Use investigation_steer to redirect its focus, or investigation_sync to download its findings.

Investigations are asynchronous: this call returns as soon as the investigation is queued, and findings appear over the following minutes.

incident_id.description: incident ID, external ID, or reference (e.g. INC-123). Starts an investigation for that incident.

tools.name: investigation_steer
tools.description:
Feed information into an in-progress investigation so it re-assesses its hypothesis.

Use this when you know something the investigation doesn't — for example, the responder has identified the real cause, telemetry shows a different explanation, or the investigation is going down the wrong path.

Provide either incident_id (ID, external ID, or reference like INC-123) or investigation_id. When using incident_id, the latest investigation is selected.

The directive should explain what the investigation should focus on and why its current hypothesis may be wrong. Good directives reference the current hypothesis and explain the correction:
- "The investigation is focused on Postgres connection pooling, but Redis connections are exhausted (100% since 14:32) — focus on Redis instead"
- "The error started immediately after the 14:30 deploy of payment-service v2.3.1 — the investigation should look at that deploy"
- "Ignore the Sentry errors — they're a known false positive from last week, not related to this incident"

Include evidence (telemetry results, log excerpts, etc.) and telemetry_query_ids when available — the investigation unpacks query IDs into rich artifacts with query expressions, datasource details, and explore URLs.

After steering, the investigation re-assesses its hypothesis within a few minutes (checks are debounced to coalesce rapid updates).

incident_id.description: incident ID, external ID, or reference (e.g. INC-123). Resolves to the latest investigation.

investigation_id.description: specific investigation ID. Use this if you already know the investigation ID.

directive.description: what the investigation should focus on and why, referencing the current hypothesis where possible. Example: 'The investigation is focused on Postgres but Redis connections are exhausted since 14:32 — focus on Redis instead'

evidence.description: supporting data as markdown — telemetry results, log excerpts, conversation context, or anything that backs up the directive

telemetry_query_ids.description: IDs of telemetry queries from ask_telemetry calls. These are unpacked into artifacts with query expressions, datasource info, and explore URLs.

tools.name: investigation_sync
tools.description:
Download an investigation as a tar.gz archive containing the full investigation filesystem.

Provide either incident_id (ID, external ID, or reference like INC-123) or investigation_id. When using incident_id, the latest investigation is selected.

The archive contains markdown files describing the investigation: findings, checks, incident context, conversation history, and more.

Optionally pass since (a timestamp) to include a preamble showing what changed since that time — useful for polling an in-progress investigation.

Returns a signed URL valid for 15 minutes.

incident_id.description: incident ID, external ID, or reference (e.g. INC-123). Resolves to the latest investigation for this incident.

investigation_id.description: specific investigation ID to download. Use this if you already know the investigation ID.

since.description: if provided, includes a preamble showing what changed since this time (RFC 3339 or any common date format)

tools.name: nexus_health_show
tools.description:
Show the health of the AI data sources the organisation has connected — the same view the dashboard's health page computes.

Each data source (telemetry, code, documents, catalog, past incidents, messages) gets a setup status (healthy, setting_up, or not_connected) and usage counts: how many distinct chats and investigations drew on it over the reported window. The telemetry and code sources break down further into per-datasource children — telemetry children carry query outcome stats (total, with data, failed, empty, cited) and attention_reasons naming what needs a human (needs_reconnection, low_success_rate, always_empty, no_active_memories, stale_guidance).

Use this when assessing whether the organisation's AI setup is working: which sources are connected but unused, which telemetry datasources are failing or never return data, and where usage concentrates. For the raw connector inventory (every datasource with its capabilities and connection status, including disabled ones), use extension_connector_list.

Health is only computed for organisations that can use investigations; otherwise data_sources is empty and message says why.

tools.name: resource_list
tools.description: List all available resources. Resources provide context that helps you use the other tools effectively — organisation config, analysis playbooks, telemetry datasources, and more. Use resource_show to read a specific resource by name.

tools.name: resource_show
tools.description:
Read a resource by name. Resources provide context that helps you use the other tools effectively. This tool returns the same content as the MCP resources, for clients that don't support the resources protocol.

Use resource_list to see all available resources, or pass one of these names:
- alert_noise_playbook: Playbook for deep alert noise analysis. Identifies noisy sources, quantifies noise cost in responder time, and produces specific tuning recommendations.
- analysis_playbook: Index of all analysis playbooks. Describes which playbook to use for different questions (operational review, alert noise, on-call burden, team health, response effectiveness). Read this first to pick the right playbook.
- metrics_glossary: Glossary of derived metrics used across playbooks: workload ratios, alert quality scores, escalation rates, and lifecycle timings. Includes formulas, interpretation guidance, and source tools.
- on_call_burden_playbook: Playbook for assessing on-call sustainability. Analyses paging volume, ack rates, overnight burden, and workload distribution across people and teams.
- onboarding_context: datasource summaries and recent successful telemetry queries
- operational_review_playbook: Playbook for periodic operational reviews (weekly/monthly/quarterly). Covers incident volume, alert noise, paging load, responder burden, and follow-up health in one comprehensive analysis.
- organisation: incident statuses, severities, roles, types, custom fields, alert priorities — discover IDs for filtering
- presenting_results_guide: Guide for structuring and formatting analysis findings. Covers output structure, formatting conventions, and the branded HTML report template.
- response_effectiveness_playbook: Playbook for measuring response effectiveness: detection speed, resolution time, escalation response, and post-incident learning outcomes.
- scope_playbook: How to establish analysis scope with the user before running a playbook. Covers goal, time window, team/org scope, comparison periods, audience, and output format. Run this first.
- team_health_playbook: Playbook for per-team or cross-team operational health assessment. Combines incident, alert, and escalation data scoped to a team.
- telemetry_datasources: connected observability platforms and their capabilities

resource.description: which resource to read — use resource_list to see all available resources

tools.name: schedule_list
tools.description:
List on-call schedules with optional search, user filter, and pagination.

Schedules define who is on call and when. Each result shows who is currently on call and how many rotations the schedule has.

Pass user (a user ID, an email address, or "me" for the caller) to answer "am I on call?" and "when am I next on call?" in one call: results narrow to schedules that user is on, and each carries the user's in-progress shift (when they are on call right now) and their next shift, looking ahead 3 months.

Use schedule_show for full details: rotation configuration, shifts over a chosen time window (past included), and when the next handover happens. List results carry no handover time.

Only native incident.io schedules are returned. When the organisation manages on-call in an external provider (e.g. PagerDuty, Opsgenie), an empty result carries a note saying so — that means we cannot see who is on call, not that nobody is.

Pagination: results are ordered by name. Use page_size (default 15, max 50) and pass "next_cursor" as "after" to fetch subsequent pages. Stopping before "has_more" is false means you have incomplete results.

after.description: cursor from a previous page to fetch the next one

user.description: a user ID, an email address, or "me" for the caller: only schedules this user is on, each carrying their current and next shift

tools.name: schedule_show
tools.description:
Look up an on-call schedule by ID and return its full details and shifts.

Returns: name, timezone, rotation configuration, and shifts for the requested window (default: now to 7 days ahead). Pass "from"/"until" to move the window — including into the past, for questions like "who was on call last Tuesday night?". Each rotation includes its users, handover frequency, working hours, current shift end, and next shift start.

When the window includes the current time, each rotation reports "current_shift_ends_at" and "next_shift_starts_at". Equal values mean someone takes over at that instant. Different values show a coverage gap. A missing current end means the rotation is not covered now; a missing next start means nothing is scheduled within the window.

Shifts created by an override carry an "override_id" — that ID is how an override is targeted later. "shifts_truncated": true means the window held more shifts than one response carries; narrow the window for the rest.

Use this to answer questions like "who's on call for the backend schedule?", "what does the rotation look like?", "when does the next handover happen?", "who is on-call next week?", or "who was on call during the incident?"

To see who would actually get paged when an alert fires, use escalation_path_show — it resolves schedules to current on-call users at each escalation level.

Only native incident.io schedules are accessible. A schedule imported from an external provider (e.g. PagerDuty, Opsgenie) returns not-found — that means we cannot read it, not that it doesn't exist.

from.description: start of the shift window (RFC 3339, e.g. 2026-08-01T00:00:00Z); defaults to now. May be in the past to read shift history

until.description: end of the shift window (RFC 3339); defaults to 7 days after from. The window may span at most 90 days

tools.name: status_page_update
tools.description:
Draft an update to a public status page for an incident: the next update when it is already published, or a first publish that creates the status page incident.

This tool only drafts. The draft is posted as a card into the conversation this call arrived from, and only a human can publish it — publishing emails or texts everyone subscribed to the page. Never tell the user an update has gone out. A caller who cannot show a publishable card is refused and told where to go instead, because a draft nobody can publish could never go live.

Action "suggest" (the default) drafts the update; "edit_suggestion" (with suggestion_id) revises an existing draft, and any field you omit keeps the draft's value. "execute" (publishing directly) is not supported yet and is refused.

For a first publish (the incident isn't on a status page yet): name is required, components must come from the page's own list, and if the organisation has more than one page the error lists them — ask the user, then pass status_page_id. When the incident is already on more than one page, pass status_page_incident_id the same way.

Write the message for customers reading the status page: lead with what they are experiencing, then what is being done about it, in plain prose that follows on from the previous updates — no internal jargon, no responder names, no incident IDs, no severity names, no internal links. Never speculate on cause, and never promise a fix time you can't evidence.

to_status moves the status page incident: investigating (something is wrong, cause unknown), identified (cause known, fix in progress), monitoring (fix applied, watching it hold), or resolved (impact over, and you're confident it is over). Keep the current status unless the evidence supports moving; moving backwards is fine when a fix didn't hold — say so in the message. For an update, only components already affected by this incident may move; resolving forces every affected component to operational.

incident_id.description: incident to draft the status page update for (ID, external ID, or reference like INC-123)

action.description: 'suggest' (default) drafts the update for a human to review and publish; 'edit_suggestion' revises an existing draft. 'execute' (publish directly) is not supported yet and is refused

suggestion_id.description: the draft to revise, required with action 'edit_suggestion' — accepts an id from a suggest result, suggestion_list, or ask_incident; omitted fields keep the draft's current values

status_page_incident_id.description: which status page incident to update. Only needed when this incident is on more than one status page, in which case a previous call will have listed the options. An edit reuses the draft's own page

status_page_id.description: which status page to publish to, for a first publish. Only needed when the organisation has more than one, in which case a previous call will have listed the options

name.description: customer-facing title for the new status page incident. Required for a first publish; ignored when updating

message.description: the update to publish, as markdown, written for customers reading the status page

to_status.description: status the status page incident moves to: investigating, identified, monitoring, or resolved. Omit to keep its current status

component_id.description: ID of a component on the status page

status.description: status this component moves to: operational, degraded_performance, partial_outage, or full_outage

component_statuses.description: status per affected component. For an update, only components already affected by this incident are accepted; for a first publish, only components on the page

tools.name: suggestion_list
tools.description:
List AI suggestions — drafts awaiting human action — with optional filters and pagination.

A suggestion is a draft the AI produced that a human accepts, edits, or declines: an incident update, summary, follow-up, escalation, or status page update. Each result carries the full drafted content (the same shape ask_incident returns), so no separate show call is needed.

Statuses:
- pending: awaiting action — these are the live drafts
- accepted / accepted_with_edits / declined: a human actioned it
- overridden: superseded by a newer suggestion or a manual update
- auto_applied: applied automatically on the org's behalf

Filters (all optional):
- incident_id: filter to a specific incident (accepts ID, external ID, or reference like INC-123). Suggestions without an incident are org-scoped and only appear when this filter is unset.
- suggestion_type: one or more of update, summary, follow_up, escalation, status_page
- status: one or more of the statuses above. Use status: ["pending"] to find live drafts — e.g. to check for an existing draft before creating another, or to find a draft's ID to edit.
- source: one or more of copilot (chatbot-drafted), copilot_edit, incident_activity, incident_update, generate_button_slack, generate_button_dashboard, request_update, orchestrator

Pagination: results are ordered newest first. Use page_size (default 10, max 50) and pass "next_cursor" as "after" to fetch subsequent pages.

To apply a pending draft, pass its id as suggestion_id with action "execute" to the tool that drafted it. Applying is real — an accepted escalation pages someone — so show the draft to a human first. Status page drafts cannot be applied this way: a human publishes them from the dashboard or Slack.

after.description: cursor from a previous page to fetch the next one

incident_id.description: filter to a specific incident (ID, external ID, or reference like INC-123)

suggestion_type.description: filter by type: update, summary, follow_up, escalation, status_page

status.description: filter by status: pending, accepted, accepted_with_edits, declined, overridden, auto_applied

source.description: filter by how the suggestion was generated, e.g. copilot, incident_activity

tools.name: team_list
tools.description:
List teams with optional name search.

Teams are catalog entries of the organisation's configured team type. Each team owns resources like escalation paths, alert sources, and schedules — use team_show to see a specific team's owned resources.

Use this tool to discover teams when scoping analysis (e.g. "which teams exist?") or to find a team by name. Pass a query to filter by name substring.

after.description: cursor from a previous page to fetch the next one

tools.name: team_show
tools.description:
Look up a team by ID and return its details with all owned resources.

Returns the team name and its owned escalation paths, alert sources, schedules, and alert routes. Use these resource IDs as filters when scoping analysis to a specific team:
- Escalation path IDs → escalation_stats(escalation_path: [...])
- Alert source IDs → alert_stats(alert_source: [...])

Use team_list to find team IDs, or check config://organisation for your own team.

id.description: team ID (the catalog entry ID for the team)

tools.name: telemetry_inspect
tools.description:
Inspect one telemetry datasource to see the real labels, label values and metric names that exist on it, so you can author a verbatim query that references things that actually exist before running it via ask_telemetry's passthrough input. This goes a level deeper than the telemetry://datasources resource: that resource lists which sources exist and their capabilities; this tool looks inside a single source you already have an ID for.

Pass a datasource_id from telemetry://datasources, then pick a kind based on that source's capabilities:
- capability "logs" → kind="log_labels", target=<stream selector> — list the label names on matching streams (set label=<name> to list that label's values). The result's syntax_hint gives the selector syntax and how to list everything when you don't know a label yet.
- capability "metrics" → kind="metric_labels", target=<metric name> — list the labels on a metric (set label=<name> to list its values).
- capability "metrics" → kind="metric_search", target=<keyword> — find metric names containing that keyword, e.g. http. The result's syntax_hint says whether finer regex matching is supported.

If a source's capabilities (in telemetry://datasources) don't include the one a kind needs, that kind isn't supported for it.

datasource_id.description: the telemetry datasource to inspect (an ID from telemetry://datasources)

kind.description: what to inspect: log_labels (a source with the logs capability), metric_labels or metric_search (a source with the metrics capability)

target.description: the anchor to inspect — log_labels: a selector for the streams to inspect, in this datasource's selector language; the result's syntax_hint gives the exact syntax and how to list everything when you don't yet know a label (active=false means the selector matched nothing — it does not say whether the label name or value was wrong); metric_labels: a metric name; metric_search: a keyword to find in metric names, e.g. http (the result's syntax_hint says whether finer regex matching is supported)

label.description: log_labels & metric_labels only: omit to list the label names on the target; set to a label name to list that label's values

filter.description: log_labels & metric_labels values mode only: case-insensitive substring filter ("-", "_", "." treated as equivalent)

tools.name: time_spent_stats
tools.description:
Break down the time responders spent working on incidents, grouped by who spent it, by time bucket, or by a custom field.

Use this to answer workload-by-person questions — "responder hours by person last quarter", "who carried the most overnight load?". Each group returns the total responder-hours spent working on incidents, split by the time of day the work happened in the responder's local time — working hours, late evening, and overnight — so you can see out-of-hours burden. It also returns the number of distinct responders in the group.

Group by (combine at most two):
- user: the responder who did the work
- week / month / quarter: time bucket
- custom_field:<field_id>: a custom field's values (read config://organisation to find field IDs)

This tool sources the per-responder hourly workload table, so it can attribute time to individual people — which incident_stats cannot. It counts time spent within the active_after/active_before window (when the work happened, not the incident's creation date), matching the time-spent Insights dashboard. To break this time down by severity, team, type or other incident attributes, use incident_stats instead — it sums whole-incident workload from the per-incident rollup.

Workload is synced hourly and may be absent for very recent activity.

group_by.description: how to group the time responders spent working on incidents. Options: user (who spent the time), week/month/quarter (time bucket), custom_field:<field_id>. Combine at most two, e.g. ["user", "month"]. If empty, returns a single total. To break this time down by severity, team or type instead, use incident_stats — it groups whole-incident workload by any incident attribute.

active_after.description: count time spent on or after this date (yyyy-mm-dd or RFC 3339). Defaults to 12 weeks before active_before.

active_before.description: count time spent before this date (yyyy-mm-dd or RFC 3339). Defaults to now.

status_category.description: filter by status category: triage, active, post-incident, closed, paused, declined, merged, canceled

incident_type.description: filter by incident type ID (read config://organisation to discover type IDs)

mode.description: filter by mode: standard, retrospective, test, tutorial

team.description: filter by team IDs (exact match). Mutually exclusive with team_part_of. Use team_list to discover team IDs.

team_part_of.description: filter by team IDs including all sub-teams in the hierarchy. Mutually exclusive with team. Use team_list to discover team IDs.

custom_fields.description: filter by custom field values: keys are custom field IDs, values are arrays of accepted value IDs

sort_groups_by.description: order groups by: alphabetical (the default — by dimension key, so time buckets come back chronological), or workload (highest total responder-hours first). max_groups keeps the first N in the current order, so for a true top-N (e.g. busiest responders) pass workload.

max_groups.description: limit the number of groups returned (e.g. top 10). Check total_groups to see how many existed before truncation. All groups are returned if omitted.

tools.name: user_list
tools.description:
List users in the organisation. Use this to find user IDs for filtering (e.g. incident_list assigned_to), assigning follow-ups, or looking someone up by name or email.

Filters (all optional):
- query: name or email substring (case-insensitive). Matched against email if the value contains "@", otherwise against display name and real name. e.g. "hannah", "hannah@incident.io".
- email: exact email match. Use when you have the full address.
- seat_type: on_call, responder, on_call_responder, viewer.

Cancels a confirmed upcoming delivery order (NOT the shopping cart). Cancel upcoming order (before picking starts). DESTRUCTIVE - requires two-step confirmation flow:
1. INQUIRY ('Can I cancel?') → call with customer_confirmed=false → returns cancellation terms/conditions
2. CONFIRMED ('Yes, cancel it') → call with customer_confirmed=true → executes cancellation
NEVER set customer_confirmed=true without prior explicit user confirmation. Not for ASAP/delivered/picking-started orders. Fetch upcoming orders first if order_id unknown.

1. INQUIRY → call with customer_confirmed=false → returns all item details and terms for review
2. CONFIRMED → call with customer_confirmed=true → executes removals sequentially with progress updates
NEVER set customer_confirmed=true without prior explicit user confirmation. Fetch order details first to get order_field_id values. Set updated_amount to 0 to remove completely, or to a lower number to reduce quantity. Items are processed one at a time; individual failures do not stop the batch.
